q: A utility company wants to estimate tomorrow's electricity use in kilowatt hours from the weather forecast. What kind of supervised task is this?
options: Regression, because the target is a continuous numeric value
Classification, because the answer falls into high, medium or low use
Classification, because weather inputs are grouped into categories
Clustering, because no labelled examples are needed for this task
explain: The target is a number on a continuous scale, so this is regression. Classification would only fit if the company chose to predict a category such as high or low use.

q: Which of these tasks is a classification problem rather than a regression problem?
options: Forecasting the travel time in minutes for a journey tomorrow
Deciding from a chest X-ray whether a patient has pneumonia
Predicting wheat yield in tonnes per hectare from soil and weather
Predicting how many support tickets will be raised tomorrow
explain: Pneumonia or no pneumonia is a discrete class. The other three predict numeric quantities, and a count of tickets is still treated as a numeric target.

q: Which statements about the labelled data used in supervised learning are correct?
options: The model learns from the features alone and never sees the labels
Labels are only needed after training is finished and are never used during it
The label is the input that the model reads in order to make a prediction
The output label is also called the dependent variable or target
Input features are also called independent variables or predictors
explain: Features are the inputs and the label is the known output the model learns to predict. The wrong options swap these roles or claim the labels are not used during learning.

q:
Is the following statement about regression correct?
"Regression returns class probabilities, and a threshold is then chosen to decide the label."
options: Correct, because every supervised model returns class probabilities first
Incorrect, because regression returns a class label and never returns a number at all
Incorrect, because that describes classification, while regression returns a number
Incorrect, because thresholds are used only in unsupervised clustering
explain: Class probabilities and thresholds belong to classification. Regression gives a number such as a price or a temperature directly.

q: A regression model makes mostly small errors but a few very large ones. Which metric will react most strongly to those few large errors?
options: Mean absolute error, because it squares each error before averaging
Mean absolute error, because it adds extra weight to the largest errors
R-squared, because it is measured in the units of the target variable
Mean squared error, because squaring penalises larger mistakes more heavily
explain: Squaring makes a large error count far more than a small one, so mean squared error is pulled up by outliers. Mean absolute error treats every unit of error equally and is less sensitive.

q: Why is root mean squared error often easier to explain to a client than mean squared error?
options: It is in the same units as the target, such as pounds or degrees
It ignores outliers completely, so it gives a steadier figure
It always lies between zero and one, which makes it easy to compare
It measures how much variance in the target the model explains
explain: Taking the square root undoes the squaring and brings the error back to the units of the target, so it reads in familiar terms. It still reacts strongly to outliers, so the option about ignoring them fails.

q: A model has an R-squared of 0. What does this tell you about the model?
options: It predicts every value perfectly, with no error at all
It does no better than always predicting the mean target value
It explains all of the variance in the target variable
It is worse than the simple baseline of always predicting the mean value
explain: A value of 1 is a perfect fit and 0 means the model adds nothing over predicting the mean. Only a value below 0 means it is worse than that baseline.

q: A model gets a negative R-squared on test data. What is the most sensible conclusion?
options: The model is a perfect fit and the negative sign is a display quirk
The model fits well, because a negative value means very low error
The model does worse than a baseline that always predicts the mean
The scoring code has a bug, because a squared value cannot be negative
explain: R-squared below 0 means the model is worse than the mean baseline. It is a warning that the model is poor, not a sign of a good fit.

q: Which of these are used to evaluate a regression model?
options: Silhouette score
Mean squared error
R-squared
Root mean squared error
Mean absolute error
explain: The four regression metrics all compare predictions with actual values. Silhouette score measures how good a clustering is, so it does not apply to regression.

q: What does ordinary least squares choose when it fits a linear regression model?
options: The coefficients that make the largest single prediction error equal to zero
The coefficients that split the data into groups of the most similar points
The coefficients that make the predictions average out to the target mean
The coefficients that minimise the sum of squared prediction errors
explain: Ordinary least squares picks the line whose predictions are closest to the data, where closeness means the smallest sum of squared residuals. It does not group data or fix one error to zero.

q: A regulator asks a team to show how each input changes the predicted price, using clear coefficients. Which model suits this best?
options: Linear regression, because it gives interpretable coefficients
Random forest regression, because averaging many trees shows each coefficient
Gradient boosting, because sequential trees give one coefficient per input
Support vector regression, because it always gives the simplest explanation
explain: Linear regression is the model used when interpretability matters and the relationship is roughly linear. Tree ensembles are accurate but do not produce simple coefficients.

q: How does a random forest regression model produce its final prediction for one case?
options: It picks the prediction of the single tree that scored best in training
It averages the numbers predicted by all of its decision trees
It lets the trees vote on a class and returns the most common class
It adds the predictions of the trees together to get one large total
explain: Each tree predicts a number and the forest returns their average. Voting is for classification, and adding without dividing would make the answer grow with the number of trees.

q: Why is a random forest usually more stable than one decision tree?
options: Each tree sees the whole dataset, so all of the trees agree and the errors vanish entirely
The trees are built one after another, each one fixing the last tree
Averaging many slightly different trees smooths out the mistakes of any one tree
The forest removes outliers from the data before any tree is built
explain: The trees are built on random rows and features, so they differ, and averaging evens out their individual errors. Building trees one after another to fix errors describes boosting instead.

q: Which statements describe how a random forest regression model is built and used?
options: The final prediction is the average of the tree predictions
It is an ensemble of many decision tree regressors
Each tree is built to correct the errors of the tree before it
It handles non-linear data well and is robust to outliers
Each tree is trained on random variations of the rows and features
explain: A random forest is an ensemble of trees, each trained on random rows and features, and it averages their predictions. It also handles non-linear data and outliers well. Correcting the errors of the previous tree is the idea behind gradient boosting, so that option is wrong.

q: How does gradient boosting regression differ from random forest regression?
options: It builds all trees at the same time on random rows and averages them
It uses a single very deep tree instead of many shallow trees
It fits a straight line through the data using least squares
It builds trees in turn, each one fixing errors left by earlier trees
explain: Random forest is a bagging method with independent trees averaged together. Boosting builds trees in sequence, each correcting the earlier ones.

q: Which of these are reasons regression models matter in research?
options: They predict continuous values such as prices and demand
They measure the effect of independent variables on an outcome
They underpin many more advanced machine learning techniques
They help test assumptions about cause and effect relationships
explain: All four are reasons given for the value of regression. It quantifies relationships, forecasts numbers, supports hypothesis testing and is a foundation for advanced models.
flag: Cause and effect wording follows the slide, in practice regression alone shows association.

q: A housing dataset has columns for square feet, bedrooms, bathrooms, location score and price. The model must predict price. Which column is the label?
options: Price, because it is the value the model is trained to predict
Square feet, because it is the first column and the most important
Location score, because it is the only column that is not a count
All the columns, because a label is any column in the dataset
explain: The label is the target output, which here is price. The other columns are input features that the model uses to estimate it.

q: A program improves its decisions by receiving rewards and penalties through trial and error, with no labelled examples. Which learning paradigm is this?
options: Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised learning
Semi-supervised learning
explain: Learning from rewards by trial and error is reinforcement learning. Supervised learning needs labelled examples and unsupervised learning looks for structure without feedback.

q: Which statements about R-squared are correct?
options: It is measured in the same units as the target variable
A value of 0 means the model is no better than predicting the mean
It shows how much of the variance in the target the model explains
A value closer to 1 means a better fit
It can never be below zero
explain: R-squared compares the model with a mean baseline and measures explained variance. It has no units and it can be negative when the model is worse than the baseline.

q: Which of these tasks are regression problems?
options: Deciding whether an email is spam
Predicting future electricity or gas consumption
Assigning a customer to a churn risk group
Identifying a dog breed from a photo
Estimating crop yield from soil and climate data
explain: Regression predicts a continuous numeric value such as consumption or yield. Spam detection, breed identification and churn grouping all choose between classes.

q: Describe the difference between classification and regression, and give one example of each.
model: Both are supervised learning tasks, which means they learn from labelled data. Classification predicts a discrete class, such as deciding whether an email is spam or not. Regression predicts a continuous numeric value, such as the price of a house from its size and location. A classification model can return probabilities for each class and a threshold turns those into a label. A regression model returns a number directly, and its quality is judged by how far the numbers are from the true values.
points: States that classification predicts discrete classes and regression predicts continuous values
Gives a correct classification example such as spam or default
Gives a correct regression example such as price or temperature
Mentions that both learn from labelled data

q: Explain what supervised machine learning is, and describe the parts of the labelled data it uses.
model: Supervised learning trains a model on labelled historical examples so it can predict the outcome for new, unseen cases. Each example has input features, also called independent variables or predictors. It also has an output label, also called the dependent variable or target. The model learns the link between the features and the label. For example, a house price model learns from past sales where size and location are the features and the sale price is the label.
points: Says the model learns from labelled examples
Names input features and output labels
Says predictions are made on new, unseen data
Gives an example that names the inputs and the output, such as house size and price

q: Explain how ordinary least squares fits a linear regression model.
model: Linear regression fits a straight line through the data, or a flat surface when there are many inputs. Ordinary least squares looks for the coefficients that place that line as close to the data as possible. It measures closeness by the residuals, which are the gaps between predicted and actual values. It squares them and adds them up, and it chooses the coefficients that make this sum as small as possible. The result is the best fitting line in the least squares sense.
points: Says the model is a line, or a flat surface for many inputs, with coefficients to find
Identifies residuals as the differences between predicted and actual values
States that the squared residuals are summed and minimised
States that the result is the line that fits the data best

q: Describe how a random forest regression model makes a prediction, and explain why this is more stable than using one decision tree.
model: A random forest is an ensemble of many decision tree regressors. Each tree is built on random rows and a random choice of features, so the trees differ from one another. For a new case every tree predicts a number. The forest returns the average of those numbers. A single tree can be thrown off by quirks in its training data, but averaging many different trees cancels out their individual errors. This makes the forest more stable, more robust to outliers and less prone to overfitting.
points: Describes many trees built on random rows and features
States that the final prediction is the average of the tree outputs
Explains that averaging reduces the effect of any one tree's errors
Mentions robustness to outliers or less overfitting

q: Compare mean absolute error with mean squared error, and say when each might be preferred.
model: Mean absolute error is the average size of the gaps between predicted and actual values. Mean squared error squares each gap before averaging, so large mistakes are penalised much more than small ones. This makes mean absolute error less sensitive to outliers and mean squared error more sensitive. If a few big errors are especially costly, mean squared error or its square root is a good choice. If outliers are rare noise and a fair typical error is wanted, mean absolute error is better.
points: Describes mean absolute error as the average size of the gaps between predicted and actual values
Describes mean squared error as squaring each gap before averaging
Says squaring penalises large errors more strongly
Says mean absolute error is less sensitive to outliers

q: Explain what R-squared tells you about a regression model, and what the values 1, 0 and below 0 mean.
model: R-squared shows how much of the variance in the target variable the model explains. A value of 1 is a perfect fit. A value closer to 1 is better. A value of 0 means the model is no better than always predicting the mean of the actual values. A value below 0 means the model is worse than that mean baseline. It is useful because it compares the model against a simple reference.
points: Says it measures the share of variance in the target explained by the model
States that 1 is a perfect fit
States that 0 equals the mean baseline
States that a negative value is worse than the baseline

q: Compare linear regression with random forest regression and explain when you would choose each.
model: Linear regression fits a straight line through the data. It works best when the relationship is roughly linear. It gives interpretable coefficients and makes a good baseline. Random forest regression averages many decision trees, so it handles non-linear patterns well, copes with outliers and is less prone to overfitting. It is less easy to interpret. I would choose linear regression when a simple explainable model is needed and the relationship looks linear. I would choose a random forest for complex, non-linear data where accuracy matters most.
points: Says linear regression suits roughly linear relationships and interpretability
Says random forest handles non-linear data and is robust
Notes the trade-off between interpretability and flexibility
Gives one situation where each model would be chosen

q: Explain the difference between random forest regression and gradient boosting regression.
model: Both use many decision trees, but they combine them differently. A random forest is a bagging method. It builds many trees independently on random variations of the data and averages their predictions. Gradient boosting builds trees one after another. Each new tree is trained to fix the errors left by the earlier trees, so the model improves step by step. Bagging mainly reduces instability, while boosting focuses on gradually correcting mistakes.
points: Identifies random forest as bagging with independent trees averaged
Identifies boosting as building trees sequentially
States that each boosted tree corrects earlier errors
Notes that both are tree ensembles
